# Two-Pass Discipline

Land a coded change in two passes: a fast first pass that sets the work down, and a slower second pass that puts it under the pressure the test runner will. The signature lives in the second pass.

## Orientation

When the project ships a layout document — README, top-level index, "getting started" file — read it once and treat the paths it names as canonical. Reading the chart and *also* reading guessed paths defeats the chart. If the working tree sits behind a network boundary, local file tools won't see it; cross with whatever transport the environment exposes.

## First pass — set it down

**Read the order verbatim.** The ticket defines the deliverable. Implement what is asked, nothing extra, no incidental cleanups, no opportunistic refactors. Files outside the order's scope are off limits, renames included.

**Branch before the first edit.**

```
git checkout -b <task-branch>
```

If earlier task branches already exist, branch off the most recent — branching off the default re-introduces work that already shipped. For a fresh repository, run `git init`, configure `user.name` and `user.email` (commits fail silently without identity), write `.gitignore`, make a scaffold commit, then branch.

**Author with byte-faithful tools.** For multi-line content, write the file as a unit and place it where it belongs — heredocs corrupt triple-quoted strings, backticks, and `$`, and "fix it later" never happens. For a single-character tweak — flipped operator, renamed identifier — an in-place stream edit is surgical; do not retransmit the whole file to change one byte.

**Commit on first contact with disk.** The earliest useful change becomes a commit *before* the tests run; what the tests reveal informs the *next* commit. Stage by exact path —

```
git add src/file.py
```

— bulk staging (`-A`) sweeps caches, build artefacts, and editor backups into the diff. One unit per commit. Don't amend, don't rebase, don't squash; uncommitted work is fragile and rewritten history is worse.

## Second pass — close it out

Walk back over the change and probe it the way the test runner will. Most failures aren't in the line you wrote — they're in the probes you skipped.

- **Concurrent access.** When two paths can mutate the same state at the same instant, they must agree on order before either commits. A read-decide-write that splits across hands corrupts state under load.
- **Repeat traffic.** Exercise the change with the call pattern the runner exercises — many invocations close together, the same input arriving through a different surface. The single happy call hides everything that breaks under repetition.
- **Bounded retention.** Any structure keyed by an ever-growing identifier — request id, session id, sliding-window key — needs a retirement rule from day one. Without one, it grows unboundedly and answers wrongly as it does.
- **Steady time source.** Elapsed-time measurements must come from a source that only moves forward. Wall-clock readings jump on daylight changes, NTP corrections, and manual resets; differences taken across them are not durations.

## Tool ordering

Group reads with known-ahead targets into one call, in parallel. A read whose path depends on the bytes of an earlier read cannot share the call. Writes invert the rule: one write, then re-inspect, then the next — concurrent writes are unrecoverable on partial failure.

## A line for whoever reads next

When the second pass turns up a defect class, a quirk, or a workaround that was non-obvious, leave one short line about it before handing off (wherever the project keeps such things, or in the commit body if there's no other channel). Name the *class* of trouble and the check that caught it — not the surface symptom of today's ticket, which won't recur. Worth-keeping lines are facts whose fix has been confirmed by a check that now passes; speculation misleads the next reader. One line per fact, edited in place, no duplicates, and never anything that `git log` would re-derive.

## Sign-off

Acting beats narrating. A prose summary isn't a deliverable; only landed commits are. A small change that landed before time ran out beats an elegant draft that didn't.
